To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the combination of pyrrole rings with thiophene units in oligomers leads to materials with higher aromatic character, higher electron affinity and lower ionization potential than the analogous oligothiophene derivatives, and that these materials can exhibit a quinoidal structure in the excited state.
the thiophene-pyrolle oligomers are highly aromatic, with an aromaticity index that increases with oligomer length, and that the aromaticity is higher for the thiophene end of the molecule.
the thiophene-pyrole oligomers are more stable in the ground state than the corresponding thiophene oligomers and that the thiophenes are more stable in their first excited states.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the electronic and structural properties of thiophene–pyrrole oligomers, with the aim of understanding their potential as organic semiconductive materials.
the development and characterization of new conjugated materials for optoelectronic applications.
the development and study of novel organic semiconducting materials based on thiophene-pyrole mixed oligomers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the combination of thiophene and pyrrole units in oligomers provides an electronic benefit that can be exploited to improve the performance of organic electronic devices.
the combination of thiophene and pyrrole in oligomers leads to an enhancement of the electronic properties, which is particularly noticeable in the solid state.
the thiophene-pyrole oligomer systems are more promising than oligothiophene systems for the development of organic semiconducting materials.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

pyrrole and thiophene are complementary in their properties, and that the combination of both heterocycles is an interesting approach to obtain materials with a good compromise between the aromatic and quinoidal character.
the thiophene-pyrole oligomers are promising candidates for organic electronic applications.
the mixed thiophene–pyrrole oligomers have an intermediate character between the two homologue series, and that they show an enhanced stability with respect to the thiophene analogues.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of thiophene and pyrrole units in oligomeric systems provides a good compromise between the electronic benefits of the two heterocycles, while avoiding their respective drawbacks.

the combination of thiophene and pyrrole units in a single oligomer leads to an increase in the electronic coupling between the heterocycles, as well as a decrease in the energy of the HOMO and LUMO levels, with respect to the analogous thiophene-based oligomers.
, in contrast to the behavior observed for oligothiophene, the introduction of a pyrrole unit in a thiophene chain does not induce a red shift in the absorption spectrum.
